subject: pathology
title: Serum Sickness, Type IV Hypersensitivity, and Contact Dermatitis

steps.tx: One to two weeks after exposure to a foreign protein or drug, circulating antigen and newly formed antibody meet in slight antigen excess and generate soluble complexes that lodge in vessel walls, joints, and glomeruli. This systemic immune complex illness is called **serum sickness**, and complement consumption with low C3 and C4 supports the diagnosis during the active phase.
steps.say: Serum sickness appears one to two weeks after the trigger, when soluble immune complexes deposit in vessels, joints, and kidneys.

nodes.label: Foreign serum or drug antigen persists in blood
IgG antibody forms soluble immune complexes
Complexes deposit in vessels, joints, glomeruli
Complement activation recruits neutrophils and injures tissue

steps.tx: This diagram is a type three reaction drawn at three addresses. In **serum sickness**, soluble antigen antibody complexes settle in a vessel wall, a joint and a glomerulus, fixing complement and recruiting neutrophils at each site. Fever, rash, aching joints and proteinuria then arrive together about ten days after the trigger. Removing the drug and supporting the patient usually suffices, because complex formation stops when antigen clears.
steps.say: Serum sickness deposits immune complexes in vessels, joints and glomeruli with complement activation. Fever, rash, joint pain and proteinuria arrive together.

vis.alt: Diagram of immune complex deposition in a vessel wall, joint and glomerulus in serum sickness.
vis.caption: Antigen antibody complexes are shown lodging in vessel, joint and kidney with complement activated. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Fever, an itchy urticarial or morbilliform rash, joint pains, and tender lymph node enlargement form the classic clinical picture that examiners expect you to recognise. The modern triggers are drugs such as equine antithymocyte globulin, antivenoms, and some antibiotics rather than the horse serum used historically, hence the modern label **serum sickness-like reaction** for drug cases without proven complexes.
steps.say: Think fever, rash, joint pains, and swollen glands about ten days after antivenom, antithymocyte globulin, or a new drug.

rows: Seven to fourteen days after exposure
Often starts near the injection site
Painful swelling of knees and small joints
Low C3 and C4, raised ESR

steps.tx: Kidney involvement decides how seriously immune complex disease is taken. **Glomerulonephritis** in serum sickness and vasculitis shows complexes and complement in glomerular filters, with haematuria, proteinuria and casts in the sediment. The urine dipstick in clinic is therefore part of grading a rash and fever illness, not an optional extra. Rising creatinine moves the same illness from symptomatic care toward immunosuppression and renal follow up.
steps.say: Immune complex glomerulonephritis adds haematuria and proteinuria to systemic vasculitis. Urine testing grades severity and the need for renal care.

vis.alt: Image of glomerulonephritis with immune deposits inflaming glomerular capillary tufts.
vis.caption: Inflamed glomeruli with immune deposits are shown in a kidney biopsy field. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Deposited complexes activate complement, release C3a and C5a, and attract neutrophils whose enzymes damage the vessel wall, producing a small vessel vasculitis with purpura in dependent skin. Immune complex vasculitis of this kind is the tissue lesion behind the rash, and the kidney may show a mild proliferative **glomerulonephritis** that settles as complexes clear.
steps.say: The rash is a small vessel vasculitis caused by complement and neutrophils attacking complex-laden vessel walls.

vis.alt: Immune complex small vessel vasculitis of skin
vis.caption: Immune complex small vessel vasculitis, the vessel lesion that produces purpuric skin rash in serum sickness.

steps.tx: Skin biopsy in immune complex disease shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis, meaning fragmented neutrophil nuclei around damaged postcapillary venules with fibrin in the wall. Direct immunofluorescence can demonstrate granular deposits of immunoglobulin and complement, a pattern pathologists call **leukocytoclastic vasculitis**, and the same granular logic explains the glomerular deposits seen on renal biopsy in systemic immune complex diseases.
steps.say: Biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with granular immunoglobulin and complement deposits in the vessel wall.

vis.caption: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis with neutrophil fragments and fibrinoid vessel wall change in immune complex skin disease.

steps.tx: Management starts with stopping the culprit drug or serum product, after which most cases settle over one to two weeks as antigen disappears and complexes are cleared by the spleen and liver. Antihistamines control itch, nonsteroidal drugs ease joint pain, and a short tapering course of **corticosteroids** is reserved for severe vasculitis, glomerulonephritis, or neurological involvement.
steps.say: Stop the trigger first; antihistamines and anti-inflammatory drugs suffice for most, with steroids kept for severe disease.

Antihistamine for itch, NSAID for joints

right.title: Severe serum sickness
points: Monitor urine, creatinine, and complement recovery

steps.tx: Unlike the antibody driven types, delayed hypersensitivity is mediated entirely by sensitised T lymphocytes and macrophages, so it peaks at forty eight to seventy two hours rather than minutes. Prior sensitisation creates memory Th1 and cytotoxic T cells that release interferon gamma on re-exposure, recruiting macrophages to the site; this mechanism is formally termed **Type IV hypersensitivity**.
steps.say: Type IV reactions are T cell driven, need no antibody, and take two to three days to reach their peak.

nodes.label: First contact sensitises Th1 and cytotoxic T cells
Re-exposure presents antigen to memory T cells
Interferon gamma recruits and activates macrophages
Indurated inflammation peaks at 48 to 72 hours

steps.tx: Check the skin exactly where jewellery touches this patient. A red, itchy patch of tiny blisters and scale maps precisely onto the contact area, sparing skin only millimetres away that never met the metal. That sharp geography marks **allergic contact dermatitis** to nickel, a delayed T cell reaction rather than an immediate antibody driven allergy of the serum sickness type.
steps.say: Where nickel jewellery touches, an itchy vesicular eczema patch appears and spares nearby untouched skin. That sharp map marks allergic contact dermatitis, a delayed T cell reaction to nickel.

vis.alt: Allergic contact dermatitis photograph showing an eczematous vesicular eruption at a nickel jewellery contact site
vis.caption: Allergic contact dermatitis photograph showing an eczematous vesicular eruption at a nickel jewellery contact site. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Nickel in jewellery, fragrances, rubber accelerators, and hair dye chemicals act as haptens that bind skin proteins and provoke an itchy eczematous eruption exactly where contact occurred, often with vesicles in acute cases. Patch testing identifies the culprit allergen, and this common occupational and cosmetic disorder is diagnosed clinically as **allergic contact dermatitis**.
steps.say: Allergic contact dermatitis gives itchy eczema at the contact site, classically from nickel, fragrances, or hair dye.

steps.tx: The tuberculin skin test is the bedside prototype of delayed hypersensitivity: intradermal purified protein derivative produces induration, not redness, measured at forty eight to seventy two hours in a sensitised person. Granulomatous inflammation in tuberculosis and sarcoidosis, graft rejection, and tumour immunity all share this **delayed-type hypersensitivity** machinery, which is why steroids and calcineurin inhibitors suppress it.
steps.say: Measure the induration of the tuberculin test at two to three days; it is the living prototype of delayed hypersensitivity.
